title: Review: Progressive waves; Electromagnetic spectrum; Polarisation; Stationary waves and harmonics; Superposition, interference and coherence
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: W03-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; W10-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; W01-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; W01-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: W01-uk1#N.10, W02-1#N.14, W10-1#N.10, W01-1#N.4, W01-uk1#N.3, W02-1#N.2, W03-1#N.8, W06-1#N.12, W10-1#N.4a, W10-uk1#N.8, W01-1#N.15, W01-uk1#N.5. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Transmission axis
items.clue: Direction in a filter along which oscillations are let through.

items.label: Node
items.clue: Point where the amplitude is zero at all times; the next one is λ/2 away.

items.label: Wavelength
items.clue: Distance between the nearest points that move in step, such as crest to crest.

items.label: Transverse wave
items.clue: Has oscillations perpendicular to the direction in which energy travels, as on a string.

questions.stem: A loudspeaker emits a steady 500 Hz note. Two microphones are placed on a straight line from the loudspeaker, 0.17 m apart. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. How do the oscillations detected by the two microphones compare?

options.text: They are in antiphase, π rad apart.
They are a quarter of a cycle, π/2 rad, apart.
They are in phase, as the note has one frequency.
They are an eighth of a cycle, π/4 rad, apart.

questions.stem: In a vacuum, the microwaves in a speed camera have a wavelength of 3.0 cm, and the light from a yellow lamp has a wavelength of 600 nm. How do their frequencies compare?

options.text: The microwave frequency is 5 × 10⁴ times the light frequency, since f rises with λ.
They are equal, because both waves travel at the same speed, c, in a vacuum.
The light frequency is 5 × 10⁴ times the microwave frequency, since f = c/λ.
The light frequency is higher, because light travels faster than microwaves.

questions.explanation: Same c for both, so f ∝ 1/λ. Ratio = (3.0 × 10⁻² m)/(600 × 10⁻⁹ m) = 5 × 10⁴: the light's frequency is that many times higher.

questions.stem: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its first harmonic. The tension in the string is then increased to four times its original value, with the length and the string unchanged. By what factor does the frequency of the first harmonic change?

options.text: ×½

questions.stem: An electric bell rings inside a sealed glass jar and can be both seen and heard. A pump gradually removes the air from the jar while the bell keeps working. Which prediction, with its explanation, is correct?

options.text: The sound fades and the bell vanishes from view, since both waves need air to travel.
Neither changes, because sound, like light, can travel through an evacuated jar.
The sound fades but the bell stays visible: light, unlike sound, needs no medium.
The sound fades but the bell stays visible, since only longitudinal waves need a medium.

questions.stem: Two points on a progressive wave of wavelength 1.2 m are 0.40 m apart along the direction of travel. What is the phase difference between their oscillations?

options.text: π/3 rad
0.33 rad
2π/3 rad
6π rad

questions.explanation: Right. Δx/λ = 0.40/1.2 = ⅓ cycle, and ⅓ × 2π = 2π/3 rad (120°).

questions.stem: Predict first. Which statement describes the nature of electromagnetic waves?

options.text: Oscillations of the particles of the medium they travel through, so they cannot cross a vacuum
Oscillating electric and magnetic fields that travel faster in a vacuum the higher their frequency
Streams of tiny charged particles given out by the source, which can travel through a vacuum
Oscillating electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel

questions.stem: Predict first. Sunlight reflected from a wet road produces glare. Polarising sunglasses reduce this glare much more than tinted sunglasses that let through the same fraction of direct sunlight. Which explanation is supported by physics?

options.text: Reflection partly polarises the light, and the lenses are oriented to block its main oscillation direction.
Reflection changes the frequency of the light, and the lenses absorb light of that changed frequency.
Reflection leaves the light unpolarised, and polarising lenses are made to block unpolarised light.
Reflected light oscillates along its direction of travel, and the lenses block light oscillating that way.

questions.stem: Two dippers vibrating in phase act as coherent sources S₁ and S₂ on a ripple tank, producing waves of wavelength 2.0 cm. Point P is 31.0 cm from S₁ and 37.0 cm from S₂. What kind of interference occurs at P?

options.text: Destructive: the paths are 15.5λ and 18.5λ, not whole numbers of λ
Destructive: the path difference, 3λ, is an odd number of λ
Neither: maxima occur only where P is equidistant from S₁ and S₂
Constructive: the path difference is 6.0 cm, which is 3λ

questions.stem: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in a standing wave. Its nodes are at x = 0, 0.40 m, 0.80 m and 1.20 m, measured from one end. Points P, Q and R on the string are at x = 0.10 m, 0.20 m and 0.70 m. Which statement about the oscillations of P, Q and R is correct?

options.text: P and Q oscillate π/4 rad out of phase, being λ/8 apart.
P and Q oscillate in phase, with amplitudes equal to each other.
P and R oscillate in antiphase, with equal amplitudes.
P and R oscillate in phase, with equal amplitudes.

questions.stem: A probe is moved between a microwave transmitter and a metal reflector. Adjacent minima of the received signal are 1.5 cm apart. What is the frequency of the microwaves?

options.text: 2.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz
4.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz
1.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz

questions.explanation: Node to node = λ/2, so λ = 3.0 cm. f = c/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 0.030 = 1.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz.

questions.stem: A vibrator sends waves along a stretched string at constant tension. At 25 Hz the wavelength is 0.80 m. The frequency is raised to 100 Hz. What is the new wavelength, and how long does a wave now take to travel 4.0 m along the string?

options.text: 0.20 m, and it takes 0.050 s
0.80 m, and it takes 0.050 s
0.20 m, and it takes 0.20 s
3.2 m, and it takes 0.20 s

questions.explanation: v = fλ = 25 × 0.80 = 20 m s⁻¹, unchanged. New λ = 20/100 = 0.20 m; time = 4.0/20 = 0.20 s, the same as before.

questions.stem: Two displacement–time graphs, P and Q, show the oscillations of two points on a wave. Both have a period of 6.0 ms. Each crest of Q comes 1.0 ms after the matching crest of P. What is the phase difference between P and Q?
